labelChirho: until / up to (temporal or spatial limit)
descriptionChirho: Preposition or conjunction marking a temporal or spatial endpoint, meaning 'until', 'up to', 'as far as'. This is the dominant usage (143x) expressing the boundary or terminus of an action or state. Multilingual evidence: Spanish 'hasta/hasta–que' (until/until that), Hindi 'तक/जब–तक' (tak = until, jab tak = until when), Arabic 'حَتَّى' (ḥattā = until), Korean '까지/–까지' (-kkaji = up to/until), Swahili 'hadi/mpaka' (until/up to). All translations uniformly employ dedicated terminative prepositions. This covers both temporal ('until the day') and spatial ('as far as Bethany') endpoints.

Conjunction introducing a temporal clause indicating duration, meaning 'while', 'as long as', 'during the time that'. This represents a distinct semantic function from the terminative 'until': rather than marking an endpoint, it describes the co-extension of two events or states. Multilingual evidence clearly differentiates this sense: Spanish 'mientras' (while/during, distinct from 'hasta'), Hindi 'जब–तक' (jab tak, with durative interpretation), Arabic 'مَا–دُمْتَ/ما–دامَ' (mā dumta/mā dāma = as long as/while, using the durative verb dāma), Korean '–동안/동안에' (dong'an = during/while, a dedicated durative marker), Swahili 'wakati' (while/when, temporal co-occurrence). The Arabic 'مَا–دُمْتَ' (as long as you remain) is particularly diagnostic of the durative rather than terminative meaning.
